headline: The FY2016 defense bill authorizes roughly a year of spending and sets rules for the military, its personnel, health care, weapons programs, and Energy Department nuclear work.
what_it_does: This law is the annual National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2016. It authorizes money for Defense Department programs such as weapons purchases, research, operations, and health care, but it does not appropriate the money itself, which happens in separate spending bills. It also sets many policies on military pay and benefits, troop levels, military justice and sexual assault response, acquisition rules, base construction, detainee transfers from Guantanamo, and Energy Department nuclear security programs. The summary covers a huge number of topics, so many provisions are reporting requirements or limits on spending until certain steps are taken.

who_it_affects.group: Active-duty service members and their families
who_it_affects.how: The law sets troop strength levels, changes pay and bonus authorities, adjusts housing allowances, and changes parts of the retirement system, including a new defined-contribution option for those who opt in.

who_it_affects.group: Military retirees and people planning to join the military
who_it_affects.how: Some provisions change retirement pay structure, survivor benefit elections, and the lump-sum and matching retirement options that apply to newer service members.

who_it_affects.group: Veterans and military members leaving service
who_it_affects.how: The law expands Yellow Ribbon reintegration eligibility, extends transition assistance training options, and changes reemployment rights for some reservists.
The law changes pharmacy cost-sharing, adds access standards and public reporting on military health care facilities, and creates some pilot programs such as urgent care without pre-authorization.

who_it_affects.group: Military sexual assault victims and service members involved in military justice
who_it_affects.how: The law expands Special Victims' Counsel services to some civilian DOD employees and changes how victims can petition courts and how certain records are kept.
The law changes acquisition rules, commercial item determinations, small business contracting goals, and surety bond guarantee amounts.
The law sets a two-year probationary period for new hires, allows delays in some step-increase pay, and extends several hiring and pay authorities.

who_it_affects.group: Residents near certain military installations and communities affected by base actions
who_it_affects.how: The law bars an additional base closure round and sets rules on some aircraft retirements and base realignments, including C-130H and A-10 units.
The law bars using Defense Department funds to transfer or release most detainees to the United States or certain countries and keeps the facility open.

who_it_affects.group: Department of Energy nuclear security workers and contractors
who_it_affects.how: The law sets new notification, bonus-restriction, and reporting rules for employees and contractors in the National Nuclear Security Administration.

when_it_takes_effect: Signed into law on November 25, 2015. Many authorizations apply to fiscal year 2016, and some provisions have later deadlines such as January 1, 2018 for the new retirement system.
